lesson_title: What the Books Still Think It's Worth: Disposal of Fixed Assets
hook_text: He sold the bakkie for R95 000. His books were expecting R103 680.
clip_script: Your uncle bought a bakkie three years ago for R180 000. Ask him what it's worth now and he says what every owner says — "about a hundred thousand, maybe." But his books have been calculating quietly the whole time, and they have an exact answer: R103 680. Then he sells it. For R95 000. He's eight thousand six hundred and eighty rand short of what the books expected — and that gap has a name: a loss on disposal. Now why can't he just write "sold, R95 000"? Because three facts about that bakkie are sitting in three different places: what he PAID, how much WEAR he's written off over three years, and what he GOT. Leave any behind and the books lie — a cost still recorded for a bakkie that's gone. So the books open a temporary desk for this one deal, put all three on it, weigh them, and clear it away the same day. And that loss? It's not a business failure. It's the books admitting their guess about wear was slightly off — and the day you sell is the day reality checks the guess.
visual_style: A bakkie on a driveway with three glowing labels lifting off it — PAID, WORN, RECEIVED — landing on a desk that tips like a scale; the shortfall highlighted as a gap before the desk folds away.
pacing: Conversational open, one number reveal, three-facts build, reflective close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and handle any disposal question a paper throws at you.
